stem: What is **coronary heart disease**?

options.content: An infection of the heart valves by bacteria carried in the blood
options.rationale: CHD is not an infection.

options.content: A hole in the septum present from birth
options.rationale: That is a different condition, present at birth.

options.content: Narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle
options.rationale: Fatty deposits reduce the blood supply to the heart muscle.

options.content: A weakness of the leg veins that makes their valves leak and the veins swell
options.rationale: This has nothing to do with the heart's blood supply.

explanation: In coronary heart disease, fatty deposits narrow or block the coronary arteries, so the heart muscle receives too little oxygen and glucose.
hints: Which arteries supply the heart muscle itself?

stem: Which of these risk factors for coronary heart disease **cannot** be changed by a person's choices?

options.content: Smoking
options.rationale: A person can choose to stop smoking.

options.content: A diet high in saturated fat
options.rationale: Diet can be changed.

options.content: Lack of exercise
options.rationale: A person can choose to exercise more.

options.content: A family history of heart disease
options.rationale: Inherited (genetic) risk cannot be changed.

explanation: Diet, smoking, exercise, body mass and stress can all be changed. Genetic predisposition (a family history), age and sex cannot, although a person with a family history can lower their overall risk by changing the other factors.
hints: Which factor is inherited?

stem: True or false: regular exercise reduces the risk of coronary heart disease.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Exercise strengthens the heart muscle, lowers blood pressure and helps keep body mass healthy.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Regular exercise strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and helps prevent obesity, all of which lower the risk.

explanation: Regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle, helps lower blood pressure, helps keep body mass healthy and can improve the balance of cholesterol in the blood, all of which reduce the risk of CHD.
hints: Think about what exercise does to blood pressure and body mass.

stem: When a coronary artery is blocked, the part of the heart muscle it supplies stops contracting. Why?

options.content: The muscle receives no oxygen or glucose, so it cannot respire to release energy.
options.rationale: Without respiration the muscle cells cannot contract, and they may die.

options.content: Blood cannot flow out of the left ventricle into the aorta to the body.
options.rationale: The chambers still contain blood; the muscle's own supply is blocked.

options.content: The valves of the heart stop closing.
options.rationale: The blockage is in a coronary artery, not in the valves.

options.content: Carbon dioxide cannot enter the muscle, so it cannot make glucose.
options.rationale: Muscle needs oxygen, not carbon dioxide.

explanation: Heart muscle needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration. If its coronary artery is blocked, it cannot release enough energy to contract, and the cells soon die: a heart attack.
hints: What do muscle cells need in order to release energy?

stem: Select **all** the factors that increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

options.content: Obesity
options.rationale: Obesity is linked to high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

options.content: A diet rich in vegetables and fruit
options.rationale: This lowers the risk.

options.content: Not smoking
options.rationale: Not smoking lowers the risk.

options.content: Smoking
options.rationale: Smoking damages the artery lining and raises blood pressure.

options.content: Regular exercise
options.rationale: Exercise lowers the risk.

options.content: A diet high in saturated fat
options.rationale: This raises blood cholesterol.

explanation: Smoking, obesity and a diet high in saturated fat all increase the risk of CHD. Regular exercise, a diet rich in vegetables and fruit, and not smoking reduce it.
hints: Three options describe healthy habits.

stem: Name the fatty substance whose high level in the blood increases the risk of fatty deposits forming in the arteries.

rejected.feedback: Glucose is a sugar, not the fatty substance in the deposits.
Fibre is not absorbed into the blood.
The deposits are mainly cholesterol and fat.

explanation: A diet high in saturated fat raises the level of cholesterol in the blood, and cholesterol builds up in the fatty deposits that narrow the arteries.
hints: It begins with 'ch'.

stem: Which of these is a cause of high blood pressure?

options.content: Eating plenty of fruit and vegetables
options.rationale: This helps to lower blood pressure.

options.content: A diet high in salt
options.rationale: Too much salt raises blood pressure.

options.content: Regular exercise
options.rationale: Exercise helps to lower blood pressure.

options.content: Drinking enough water
options.rationale: Drinking water does not cause high blood pressure.

explanation: A diet high in salt is one cause of high blood pressure. Others include inheritance, stress, lack of exercise, obesity, smoking, too much alcohol and ageing.
hints: Which item in the diet is linked to blood pressure?

stem: Blood pressure readings that are repeatedly 140/90 mmHg or higher are usually counted as high blood pressure. Four adults had their blood pressure checked at a clinic in Mutare. Whose reading is in the high range?

options.content: Tendai: 118/76 mmHg
options.rationale: Both numbers are well below 140/90.

options.content: Rudo: 125/82 mmHg
options.rationale: Both numbers are below 140/90.

options.content: Mr Moyo: 152/96 mmHg
options.rationale: Both numbers are above 140/90.

options.content: Chipo: 110/70 mmHg
options.rationale: This is a low-normal reading.

explanation: Only Mr Moyo's reading (152/96 mmHg) is above 140/90. A single high reading should be checked again, because blood pressure varies; repeated high readings mean high blood pressure.
hints: Compare both numbers with 140/90.

stem: Complete the sentences about coronary heart disease.

payload.template: Fatty deposits build up in the walls of the {{blank:art}} arteries. The lumen of each artery becomes {{blank:nar}}, so less {{blank:oxy}} reaches the heart muscle.

explanation: In CHD, fatty deposits narrow the lumen of the coronary arteries, so less blood, and therefore less oxygen and glucose, reaches the heart muscle.
hints: Which arteries supply the heart muscle?

stem: Why does a diet high in saturated fat increase the risk of coronary heart disease?

options.content: Saturated fat blocks the stomach, so less food is absorbed.
options.rationale: Fat does not block the gut.

options.content: It raises blood cholesterol, so fatty deposits build up in the artery walls.
options.rationale: These deposits narrow the coronary arteries.

options.content: Saturated fat is turned into salt, which raises blood pressure.
options.rationale: Fat is not turned into salt.

options.content: Saturated fat makes the blood too thin to clot.
options.rationale: The problem is fatty deposits and clots in the arteries.

explanation: A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol. Cholesterol builds up in the inner walls of arteries as fatty deposits, narrowing the coronary arteries and making clots more likely.
hints: What substance builds up in the fatty deposits?

stem: Which statement best explains how regular exercise lowers the risk of coronary heart disease?

options.content: Exercise uses up all the cholesterol in the body.
options.rationale: Cholesterol is still present and needed; exercise helps the balance, it does not remove it all.

options.content: Exercise makes the coronary arteries grow wider and wider every day.
options.rationale: Exercise does not simply widen the arteries each day.

options.content: Exercise stops the heart from needing oxygen.
options.rationale: Heart muscle always needs oxygen.

options.content: It strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and helps keep body mass healthy.
options.rationale: All three lower the risk.

explanation: Regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle, helps reduce blood pressure, helps prevent obesity and can improve blood cholesterol, all of which reduce the risk of fatty deposits and clots in the coronary arteries.
hints: Think about the heart muscle, blood pressure and body mass.

stem: In a hypothetical study, 6 in every 1000 adults who exercised regularly developed CHD within ten years, compared with 15 in every 1000 adults who did no exercise. How many times greater was the rate among the adults who did no exercise?
explanation: $\dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5$, so the rate was 2.5 times greater in the adults who did no exercise. This shows a link (correlation) between lack of exercise and CHD.
workedSolution: 1. Divide the larger rate by the smaller: $\dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5$.
hints: Divide one rate by the other.

stem: A patient's blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg. After six months of treatment and a low-salt diet it was 140/88 mmHg. Calculate the percentage fall in the higher (systolic) reading.
explanation: Fall $= 160 - 140 = 20$ mmHg. Percentage fall $= \dfrac{20}{160} \times 100 = 12.5\%$.
hints: Divide the fall by the original reading.

stem: True or false: a survey found that people who ate more fried food had more heart disease. This alone proves that fried food causes heart disease.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. A survey like this shows a correlation; other factors (such as smoking or exercise) might explain it.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. It shows a correlation only. People who eat more fried food might also smoke more or exercise less.

explanation: A survey that finds two things together shows a correlation, not a cause. To support a causal link, other risk factors must be allowed for, many studies should agree and a mechanism should be known.
hints: What is the difference between a correlation and a cause?

stem:
The table shows hypothetical results of a ten-year study of adults grouped by how much moderate exercise they took each week.

| Exercise per week | Number of adults | Number who developed CHD | Percentage who developed CHD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 1200 | 84 | ? |
| 1–2 hours | 1500 | 75 | 5.0 |
| 3–4 hours | 900 | 27 | 3.0 |
| 5 hours or more | 400 | 8 | 2.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the missing percentage for the adults who took no exercise.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the relationship between exercise and the percentage of adults who developed CHD.

points.description: The more exercise per week, the lower the percentage who developed CHD (negative correlation)
Quotes data, e.g. 7.0% with no exercise falling to 2.0% with 5 hours or more

parts.explanation: The more exercise the adults took, the smaller the percentage who developed CHD: 7.0% of those who took none, falling to 2.0% of those who exercised for 5 hours or more a week.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how regular exercise could reduce the risk of CHD.

points.description: Strengthens heart muscle / heart pumps more blood per beat
Lowers blood pressure / helps maintain a healthy body mass / improves blood cholesterol, so fewer fatty deposits form

parts.explanation: Exercise strengthens the heart muscle and helps lower blood pressure and keep body mass healthy, so fatty deposits are less likely to build up in the coronary arteries.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** other factors that should be similar in the groups before concluding that exercise reduces the risk.

points.description: Smoking
Diet (saturated fat, salt)
Age / sex / family history (genes) / body mass / stress

parts.explanation: For example: how many people in each group smoked, and their diets. Age, sex, family history and body mass could also differ between the groups.

explanation: (a) $\dfrac{84}{1200} \times 100 = 7.0\%$. The percentage falls as exercise increases, a negative correlation. Exercise strengthens the heart and lowers blood pressure and body mass, but other factors such as smoking and diet must be similar before concluding that exercise is the cause.
hints: Percentage = number who developed CHD ÷ number in the group × 100.
Think of the other risk factors for CHD.

stem: Mr Dube is 55. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day, works long hours in a stressful job and eats fried food and fatty meat most days. He is overweight and rarely exercises. His father died of a heart attack at the age of 60.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify **three** of Mr Dube's risk factors that he could change.

points.description: Smoking
Diet high in (saturated) fat / fried food
Lack of exercise
Being overweight (obesity)
Stress

parts.explanation: Any three of: smoking, a diet high in saturated fat (fried food and fatty meat), lack of exercise, being overweight and stress.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which of his risk factors can he **not** change?

options.content: Being overweight and taking little exercise
options.rationale: He can lose mass and exercise more.

options.content: His father's history of heart disease and his age
options.rationale: Inherited risk and age cannot be changed.

options.content: His smoking and his long hours in a stressful job
options.rationale: He can stop smoking and reduce his stress.

options.content: His diet of fried food and fatty meat
options.rationale: He can change what he eats.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest how stopping smoking would reduce his risk of a heart attack.

points.description: Less damage to the lining of the arteries / fewer fatty deposits and clots
Lower heart rate and blood pressure (no nicotine) / more oxygen carried by the blood (no carbon monoxide)

parts.explanation: Without smoke, the lining of his arteries would be damaged less and clots would form less easily, and without nicotine his heart rate and blood pressure would fall; his blood would also carry more oxygen without carbon monoxide.

explanation: Smoking, a fatty diet, lack of exercise, being overweight and stress are risk factors he can change; his family history and age cannot be changed. Stopping smoking reduces damage to the arteries, clotting, heart rate and blood pressure.
hints: Separate lifestyle choices from things he was born with or cannot alter.

stem: Describe how coronary heart disease develops and explain how it can lead to a heart attack. [5]

points.description: Fatty deposits (containing cholesterol) build up in the walls of the coronary arteries
The lumen narrows (and the wall becomes rough / less elastic)
Less blood flows to the heart muscle, so it gets less oxygen and glucose
A blood clot forms on the deposit and blocks the artery
Heart muscle beyond the blockage cannot respire (aerobically), so it stops contracting / dies: a heart attack

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Fatty deposits containing cholesterol build up in the inner walls of the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle. The lumen becomes narrower and the wall rough, so less blood, and therefore less oxygen and glucose, reaches the heart muscle. A blood clot may form on the rough surface of a deposit and block the artery completely. The heart muscle beyond the blockage then receives no oxygen, cannot respire aerobically, stops contracting and may die. This is a heart attack.

explanation: CHD is a chain: deposits → narrowed coronary artery → less oxygen and glucose to the heart muscle → clot → complete blockage → heart attack.
hints: Begin with fatty deposits and end with heart muscle dying.

stem: Discuss the roles of diet and exercise in reducing the risk of coronary heart disease. [6]

points.description: Eating less saturated fat lowers blood cholesterol
so fewer fatty deposits form in the coronary arteries
Eating less salt helps keep blood pressure down
Balancing energy intake with energy use prevents obesity (more fruit, vegetables and fibre)
Exercise strengthens the heart muscle
Exercise lowers blood pressure / helps control body mass / improves cholesterol balance
Limitation: diet and exercise cannot remove inherited risk, age or sex; smoking and stress also matter, so they reduce but do not remove the risk

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Diet affects the risk in several ways. Eating less saturated fat (fatty meat, butter, fried food) lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood, so fewer fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries. Eating less salt helps keep blood pressure down, which reduces damage to artery walls. Matching energy intake to energy use, with plenty of vegetables, fruit and fibre, helps prevent obesity. Regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle, helps lower blood pressure, helps keep body mass healthy and can improve the balance of cholesterol. However, diet and exercise reduce the risk rather than remove it: inherited factors, age and sex cannot be changed, and smoking and stress must also be tackled.

explanation: A 'discuss' answer explains how each of diet and exercise lowers the risk and recognises the limits (genes, age, sex, other factors).
hints: Give at least two points about diet and two about exercise.
End with a limitation.

stem: Farai's coronary arteries are partly narrowed. He has no pain at rest, but he gets chest pain when he climbs a steep hill. What is the best explanation?

options.content: During exercise his heart muscle needs more oxygen than the narrowed arteries can deliver.
options.rationale: At rest the reduced supply is just enough; during exercise it is not.

options.content: Climbing makes his blood too thick to flow.
options.rationale: Exercise does not thicken the blood in this way.

options.content: His lungs stop working when he exercises.
options.rationale: His lungs work; the problem is the heart's own blood supply.

options.content: The narrowed arteries become completely blocked every time he exercises.
options.rationale: A complete blockage would cause a heart attack, not pain that stops with rest.

explanation: When Farai exercises, his heart beats faster and harder, so its muscle needs more oxygen and glucose. The narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough, so the muscle is short of oxygen and he feels chest pain, which eases when he rests.
hints: Does the heart muscle need more oxygen at rest or during exercise?

stem: Which is an effect of high blood pressure that is not treated?

options.content: It strengthens the walls of the arteries, so they are less likely to burst.
options.rationale: High pressure damages artery walls.

options.content: It lowers the risk of a stroke.
options.rationale: It raises the risk of a stroke.

options.content: It makes the heart work less hard to pump blood round the body.
options.rationale: The heart has to work harder against high pressure.

options.content: It damages artery walls, raising the risk of heart disease and stroke.
options.rationale: Damaged walls collect fatty deposits more easily, and brain arteries may burst.

explanation: High blood pressure makes the heart work harder and damages the walls of arteries, so fatty deposits form more easily (raising the risk of CHD); arteries in the brain may also burst or be blocked, causing a stroke. The kidneys can be damaged too.
hints: Think about the stress on the walls of the arteries.

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: Damage to or death of part of the heart muscle when a coronary artery is blocked
Damage to the brain when an artery in the brain is blocked or bursts
Something that increases the chance of developing a disease
A fatty substance in the blood that builds up in deposits in artery walls
An infection of the lungs caused by bacteria

explanation: A heart attack affects the heart muscle; a stroke affects the brain; a risk factor raises the chance of disease; cholesterol builds up in fatty deposits. The lung infection does not match any term.
hints: One description does not match any of the terms.

stem:
Twenty office workers in Harare who took little exercise joined a 12-week programme of brisk walking for 40 minutes a day. Their mean values were measured before and after the programme. (The data are hypothetical.)

| Measurement | Before | After 12 weeks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resting heart rate / beats per minute | 78 | 70 |
| Systolic blood pressure / mmHg | 138 | 128 |
| Blood cholesterol / mmol per dm³ | 6.2 | 5.6 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage decrease in blood cholesterol. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how a fall in blood cholesterol could reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.

points.description: Less cholesterol builds up as fatty deposits in the walls of the coronary arteries
so the arteries are less likely to be narrowed or blocked by a clot, and the heart muscle keeps its oxygen supply

parts.explanation: With less cholesterol in the blood, fewer fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries, so they are less likely to become narrowed or blocked by a clot, and the heart muscle keeps its supply of oxygen and glucose.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why the resting heart rate fell.

points.description: Exercise strengthened the heart muscle
so more blood is pumped with each beat and fewer beats are needed at rest

parts.explanation: Regular exercise strengthened the heart muscle, so it pumps more blood with each beat and needs fewer beats per minute at rest.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons why these results do not prove that walking alone caused the changes.

points.description: No control group of similar people who did not walk
Small sample (twenty people)
Other changes may have happened at the same time, e.g. diet, smoking, stress or body mass

parts.explanation: There was no control group of similar workers who did not walk, the sample was small, and the workers may also have changed their diet, smoking or stress levels during the 12 weeks.

explanation: Cholesterol fell by $6.2 - 5.6 = 0.6$ mmol per dm³, which is $\dfrac{0.6}{6.2} \times 100 = 9.7\%$. Lower cholesterol means fewer fatty deposits in the coronary arteries; a stronger heart pumps more per beat, so the resting rate falls. Without a control group, and with only twenty people, other factors cannot be ruled out.
hints: Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ starting value × 100.
What would a fair comparison need?
